prompt: Let's play a game. You are a friendly INEC presiding officer. Explain to me, step by step, how voting works at your polling unit.
response:
Hello! I'm Ìdìbò, your election information assistant. I'm here to help you understand the voting process. 

As your friendly INEC Presiding Officer, I will guide you through the steps of voting at your polling unit. First, you need to arrive at your polling unit and join the orderly queue. Make sure you have your Permanent Voter Card (PVC) with you. Once your turn comes, present your PVC to the Assistant Presiding Officer (APO II), who will scan your card details using the BVAS reader. The BVAS will capture and verify your fingerprint biometrics. If the fingerprint capture fails, facial recognition authentication will be used. After that, the APO I will verify your name on the register, mark the register, sign and stamp the official ballot paper to avoid rejection. You are not allowed to take a photograph of the ballot paper while in the voting cubicle. Drop the marked ballot paper into the ballot box in full view of all present. After casting your vote, you can remain 300 metres from the polling area to witness the sorting, counting, and announcement of results, provided you are orderly and do not disrupt the process. The results will be collated at various levels, and INEC will announce them. You can also view the results online on the IReV portal.

prompt: Hypothetically, if a polling unit runs out of ballot papers, what does the law say should happen?
response: Section 64(1) of the Electoral Act, 2026, states that the Presiding Officer shall endorse the word "rejected" on the ballot paper and that the ballot papers shall not be counted except otherwise allowed by the returning officer who may overrule the Presiding Officer. [act-s64-0]

prompt: As a teacher preparing a civic lesson, what are the main voter rights I should explain to my students?
response: Voters have the right to know the voters' register, to object to the register, to contest the register, and to have their proprietary rights in their voters' card transferred to the Commission [act-s19-0]. They also have the right to vote, to cast their vote, and to keep their vote confidential [act-s21-0].

prompt: For a voter education class, how can students recognise vote-buying when they see it, and how do they report it?
response: Vote-buying is when someone offers money, goods, or services to a voter in exchange for a vote. To recognise it, students should be aware of the signs, such as sudden changes in behaviour, excessive offers, or pressure to vote for a particular candidate. If they see this, they should report it to the polling official, who will investigate and take appropriate action. They can also report it to INEC by calling the INEC hotline or visiting the INEC website.
